title: Gangsters, Prohibition and who ran the State Street clubs
summary: He says gangsters did not run the Black-owned clubs, which were run by Black proprietors; gangsters ran places around 22nd.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: In the old days here in Chicago, were there many gang fights around when you were playing here in the Prohibition? No, no. Has Al Capone taken over yet or not? No, no. I never, never saw a fight.

They didn't do any fighting much around there. They just got to their man. If they'd get caught their man in one of those places, wouldn't be no much of a fight. Those fellas, you see, they didn't do much fighting. They just got the man. Yeah.
When he's mobbed, he's mobbed, he's mobbed.

Took them for a ride. The only way he could have any more success in life is to leave town. Yeah. High grossing moustaches and whiskers and something, disguise himself. Because they'd get you, you could not get away once you were mobbed. And then they didn't bother no strangers.
Did the gangsters control the dance halls? Who ran the E-Light in all those places?
Art Cardoza and Tina and Jones run the E-Light. Bill Bottoms run the Dreamlin. And Frank Preyer run the Deluxe, by the way I tell you.
Were most of those people colored? Colored, yes.
They were colored. They all colored.
So it wasn't any gangster control then. Oh no.
They were, we used to love to see the gangsters, so-called gangsters coming in, because they were the best tempers.
Yeah. But they didn't own the places that run them then.
No, they didn't run any of these places. The places they run was down around 22nd. Yeah. We used to go down there, down to Big Jim Colosimo.
Oh yeah, I've heard of that. Yeah. Yeah. But they didn't run the E-Light or Royal Garden or Dreamland and those places.
